title: Natural Vegetation Dynamics Confound the Impact of Ecological Restoration on Dryland Hydrology
content:
Abstract

Large-scale ecological restoration (ER) projects have increased shrub and grass cover and growth in arid and semi-arid regions, but concurrently reduced terrestrial water storage (TWS) through enhanced evapotranspiration (ET). However, the impact of ER on TWS remains unclear due to the confounding effect of natural vegetation dynamics (driven by climate change, distinct from direct land-use change). To address this issue, we integrated the ecohydrological model Tethys–Chloris (T&C) with the dynamic vegetation model Cellular Automata Tree–Grass–Shrub Simulator (CATGraSS). This integration framework enabled a process-based assessment to disentangle the impacts of ER from those of natural vegetation cover expansion (NVE) and natural vegetation growth (NVG), with the latter defined as changes in leaf area density and biomass per unit vegetation cover. We applied this framework to Mu Us Sandyland in China, a typical semi-arid region undergoing ecological restoration. Our results show that ER reduced TWS at a rate of −5.16 mm/yr, while NVE and NVG contributed −1.58 and −0.66 mm/yr, respectively. Adopting the conventional static vegetation assumption—which ignores natural vegetation dynamics (NVE and NVG) by assuming that post-ER vegetation conditions remain at pre-ER averages—would overestimate the ER-induced TWS depletion by 43.4%, a bias primarily resulting from misattributing the increases in transpiration and declines in soil evaporation caused by natural vegetation dynamics to those caused by ER. Our findings have general implications as they underscore the critical necessity of integrating natural vegetation processes into ER impact assessments to correctly attribute impacts and support sustainable water resources management in water-limited ecosystems.
